Guide previously added a <5 mg/dL target for tophaceous gout; the guideline explicitly declines to set a lower threshold, so the guide now says so.

claims.text: Allopurinol is the long-term urate-lowering drug; flare pain is treated with colchicine, an NSAID, or a steroid (not interchangeable)
claims.quote: Using colchicine, NSAIDs, or glucocorticoids (oral, intraarticular, or intramuscular) as appropriate first-line therapy for gout flares over IL-1 inhibitors or adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) is strongly recommended for patients experiencing a gout flare.

claims.text: Allopurinol is not a flare treatment; colchicine is an anti-inflammatory rather than a urate-lowering drug (key takeaway, two-jobs section, mistakes list, FAQ on colchicine and uric acid)
claims.quote: Administering concomitant antiinflammatory prophylaxis therapy (e.g., colchicine, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs [NSAIDs], prednisone/prednisolone) over no antiinflammatory prophylaxis therapy is strongly recommended.

claims.text: Allopurinol is started low (100 mg daily or less, lower in chronic kidney disease) and titrated
claims.quote: Starting treatment with low-dose allopurinol (≤100 mg/day and lower in patients with CKD [stage ≥3]) and febuxostat (≤40 mg/day) with subsequent dose titration over starting at a higher dose is strongly recommended.

claims.text: Titrate to a serum urate below 6 mg/dL for all patients on urate-lowering therapy
claims.quote: Achieving and maintaining an SU target of <6 mg/dl over the use of no target is strongly recommended for all patients receiving ULT.

claims.text: The guideline does not set a lower threshold for tophaceous gout and notes no trial data support one
claims.quote: this guideline does not specify SU thresholds beyond <6 mg/dl for patient subsets with more severe disease (e.g., those with tophi).

claims.text: No trial data for lower thresholds
claims.quote: there are no trial data to support lower specific thresholds for such patients.

claims.text: Serum urate is checked after each dose change
claims.quote: SU concentrations should be checked after each dose titration

claims.text: Allopurinol is preferred first-line, including for people with moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease
claims.quote: Treatment with allopurinol as the preferred first-line agent, over all other ULTs, is strongly recommended for all patients, including those with moderate-to-severe CKD (stage ≥3).

claims.text: Prophylaxis with colchicine, an NSAID, or prednisone for at least 3 to 6 months when urate-lowering therapy starts reduces early flares
claims.quote: When initiating ULT, concomitant antiinflammatory prophylaxis therapy for a duration of at least 3-6 months was strongly recommended.

claims.text: Prophylaxis continued longer if flares persist; prophylaxis is added to limit flares when urate-lowering therapy starts
claims.quote: these guidelines reinforce prior recommendations to use concurrent antiinflammatory prophylaxis for 3–6 months’ duration, a shorter duration than advocated for in prior recommendations, but one that should be extended in the setting of frequent ongoing flares.

claims.text: Continue prophylaxis for 3 to 6 months rather than less than 3 months, with ongoing evaluation (together section, FAQ on stopping colchicine)
claims.quote: Continuing concomitant antiinflammatory prophylaxis therapy for 3–6 months over <3 months, with ongoing evaluation and continued prophylaxis as needed if the patient continues to experience gout flares, is strongly recommended.

claims.text: A lower starting dose reduces flares at initiation
claims.quote: A lower starting dose of any ULT reduces the risk of flare associated with initiation

claims.text: A lower starting dose mitigates allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome risk
claims.quote: Using a lower starting dose mitigates safety issues specific to allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS)

claims.text: Urate falls as the dose is titrated over weeks to months
claims.quote: ULT titration should occur over weeks to months, not years.

claims.text: HLA-B*58:01 testing conditionally recommended before allopurinol in Southeast Asian descent (e.g., Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) and African American patients
claims.quote: Testing for the HLA–B*5801 allele prior to starting allopurinol is conditionally recommended for patients of Southeast Asian descent (e.g., Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) and for African American patients

claims.text: Febuxostat carries an FDA boxed warning
claims.quote: interest to provide recommendations consistent with the FDA black box warning for febuxostat

claims.text: Switching away from febuxostat is conditionally recommended with a history of cardiovascular disease or a new event
claims.quote: Switching to an alternative oral ULT agent, if available and consistent with other recommendations in this guideline, is conditionally recommended for patients taking febuxostat with a history of CVD or a new CVD-related event.

claims.text: Continuing urate-lowering therapy indefinitely is conditionally recommended (mistakes list, FAQ on how long)
claims.quote: Continuing ULT indefinitely over stopping ULT is conditionally recommended.

claims.text: In people who stopped urate-lowering therapy, higher urate went with more frequent flares
claims.quote: patients with higher SU concentrations after withholding therapy had more frequent flares with greater likelihood of flares associated with higher SU levels

claims.text: When urate-lowering therapy is indicated during a flare, starting it during the flare is conditionally recommended
claims.quote: When the decision is made that ULT is indicated while the patient is experiencing a gout flare, starting ULT during the gout flare over starting ULT after the gout flare has resolved is conditionally recommended.

claims.text: The ACR guideline strongly recommends low-dose over high-dose colchicine
claims.quote: Given similar efficacy and a lower risk of adverse effects, low-dose colchicine over high-dose colchicine is strongly recommended when colchicine is the chosen agent.

claims.text: Allopurinol is titrated on measured urate (red flags paragraph)
claims.quote: A treat-to-target management strategy that includes ULT dose titration and subsequent dosing guided by serial SU measurements to achieve a target SU, over a fixed-dose ULT strategy, is strongly recommended for all patients receiving ULT.

claims.text: Low-dose course (1.8 mg over 1 hour) versus high-dose course (4.8 mg over 6 hours)
claims.quote: compared self-administered low-dose colchicine (1.8 mg total over 1 hour) and high-dose colchicine (4.8 mg total over 6 hours) with placebo.

claims.text: Low-dose colchicine gave pain relief comparable to high-dose, with side effects similar to placebo
claims.quote: Low-dose colchicine yielded both maximum plasma concentration and early gout flare efficacy comparable with that of high-dose colchicine, with a safety profile indistinguishable from that of placebo.

claims.text: AGREE chart: 37.8%, 32.7%, 15.5% with at least 50% pain reduction at 24 hours
claims.quote: Responders included 28 of 74 patients (37.8%) in the low-dose group, 17 of 52 patients (32.7%) in the high-dose group, and 9 of 58 patients (15.5%) in the placebo group

claims.text: High-dose course caused far more diarrhea and vomiting
claims.quote: With high-dose colchicine, 40 patients (76.9%) had diarrhea (OR 21.3 [95% CI 7.9-56.9]), 10 (19.2%) had severe diarrhea, and 9 (17.3%) had vomiting. With low-dose colchicine, 23.0% of the patients had diarrhea

claims.text: Flare dose 1.2 mg at first sign, then 0.6 mg one hour later
claims.quote: is 1.2 mg (two tablets) at the first sign of the flare followed by 0.6 mg (one tablet) one hour later

claims.text: Adult prophylaxis 0.6 mg once or twice daily
claims.quote: for adults and adolescents older than 16 years of age is 0.6 mg once or twice daily

claims.text: Maximum prophylaxis dose 1.2 mg per day
claims.quote: The maximum recommended dose for prophylaxis of gout flares is 1.2 mg/day.

claims.text: Mechanism: blocks microtubule formation, preventing neutrophil activation and migration thought to mediate gout symptoms; may interfere with the inflammasome
claims.quote: colchicine disrupts cytoskeletal functions through inhibition of β-tubulin polymerization into microtubules and consequently prevents the activation, degranulation and migration of neutrophils thought to mediate some gout symptoms.

claims.text: Possibly interfering with the inflammasome
claims.quote: evidence suggests that colchicine may interfere with the intracellular assembly of the inflammasome complex present in neutrophils and monocytes that mediates activation of interleukin-1β.

claims.text: Colchicine is not a urate-lowering drug; it is used alongside urate-lowering therapy
claims.quote: Colchicine tablets are recommended upon initiation of gout flare prophylaxis with uric acid-lowering therapy.

claims.text: Severe kidney impairment: prophylaxis starting dose 0.3 mg per day
claims.quote: in patients with severe impairment, the starting dose should be 0.3 mg/day

claims.text: Severe kidney impairment: flare course repeated no more than once every two weeks
claims.quote: a treatment course should be repeated no more than once every two weeks.

claims.text: Dialysis: single 0.6 mg dose for a flare
claims.quote: the total recommended dose for the treatment of gout flares should be reduced to a single dose of 0.6 mg (one tablet).

claims.text: Doses adjusted for interacting drugs (CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitors)
claims.quote: Coadministration of colchicine tablets with drugs known to inhibit CYP3A4 and/or P-glycoprotein (P-gp) increases the risk of colchicine-induced toxic effects (Table 1).

claims.text: Colchicine is a P-gp and CYP3A4 substrate; fatal interactions reported
claims.quote: Colchicine is a P-gp and CYP3A4 substrate. Life-threatening and fatal drug interactions have been reported in patients treated with colchicine

claims.text: Examples: clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and other HIV protease inhibitors, cyclosporine
claims.quote: Clarithromycin; Itraconazole; Ketoconazole; Ritonavir; Cyclosporine

claims.text: Contraindicated with kidney or liver impairment
claims.quote: Patients with renal or hepatic impairment should not be given colchicine tablets in conjunction with P-gp or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (this includes all protease inhibitors except fosamprenavir).

claims.text: Fatal overdoses reported
claims.quote: Fatal overdoses, both accidental and intentional, have been reported in adults and children who have ingested colchicine

claims.text: Most common side effect during flare treatment is diarrhea
claims.quote: for treatment of gout flares were diarrhea (23%) and pharyngolaryngeal pain (3%).

claims.text: Red flag: muscle pain or weakness, tingling or numbness in fingers or toes; stop and seek care
claims.quote: muscle pain or weakness, tingling or numbness in fingers or toes may occur with colchicine tablets alone ... must discontinue colchicine tablets and seek medical evaluation immediately.

claims.text: Dose reduction considered in severe hepatic impairment
claims.quote: Dose reduction should be considered for the prophylaxis of gout flares in patients with severe hepatic impairment
